Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

ecodive 2.4.0

  • ecodive now covers a whole diversity analysis: besides alpha and beta diversity, it ordinates samples and tests what explains their distances (see below). New vignettes, vignette("ordination") and vignette("stat_tests"), walk through both, and the README and vignette("ecodive") give an overview of everything the package does. The package title is now “Parallel and Memory-Efficient Ecological Diversity Analysis”.

  • New pcoa() runs a principal coordinates analysis (classical multidimensional scaling) on a dist object, such as from beta_div(). It gives the same coordinates and eigenvalues as cmdscale(), ape::pcoa(), and vegan::wcmdscale() (up to each axis’s sign), but computes only the first few axes (n_axes = 3 by default), in parallel C, without forming an n-by-n matrix. Its results are identical for any number of cpus. correction = "lingoes" or "cailliez" adds the smallest constant to the squared distances, or to the distances, that leaves no negative eigenvalue, giving the same constants, eigenvalues and coordinates as ape::pcoa(), vegan::wcmdscale(add = ) and cmdscale(add = TRUE), again without an n-by-n (or 2n-by-2n) matrix: with 2,000 samples, "cailliez" takes 20 seconds where cmdscale(add = TRUE) takes 2 minutes. Every result has correction and constant attributes.

  • New pcoa_biplot() projects the features of a table (taxa counts, or environmental variables) onto the axes of a pcoa() result, for drawing arrows on a PCoA plot. It computes the same scores as scikit-bio’s pcoa_biplot(), in parallel C, keeps sparse tables sparse, and takes every table type and norm that pca() does. envfit() gives the same directions with permutation tests.

  • Every ordination function takes the number of axes to return as n_axes (3 by default for the methods whose axes have eigenvalues: pcoa(), pca(), rpca(), dbrda(), capscale() and isomap(); 2 for mds(), nmds(), tsne() and umap()). The name says what it counts; k, as cmdscale() and vegan call it, often means a number of neighbours in these methods.

  • New dist_ord() runs any distance-based ordination method by name, as beta_div() does for beta diversity metrics and dist_test() does for statistical tests, with the method’s own arguments: dist_ord(dm, "nmds") is nmds(dm). list_dist_ords() and match_dist_ord() list and look up the methods. count_ord(), with list_count_ords() and match_count_ord(), does the same for the methods that take a count table rather than distances, pca(), rda(), cca(), ca(), lda(), plsda(), oplsda() and rpca(): count_ord(counts, "pca") is pca(counts). Each wrapper points to the other when given the other’s method, and to dist_test() when given a test. Every ordination method returns the same kind of result: a sample-by-axis matrix (of class "ecodive_ord", which prints its attributes’ names rather than their contents) whose attributes start with method, eig, and prop. Every method rejects negative distances (beyond rounding error), and seed can be given to any of them through dist_ord().

  • New nmds() runs non-metric multidimensional scaling with the SMACOF algorithm of scikit-learn’s non-metric MDS(), ported to parallel C. It starts from the PCoA solution and from n_starts random configurations, keeps the one with the lowest Kruskal stress-1, and centers it, rotates it to principal axes, and scales it to the distances. Tied distances use Kruskal’s primary approach (as in vegan::metaMDS()), or scikit-learn’s secondary one with ties = "secondary". The distances are sorted once and shared by all starts; nothing n-by-n is formed. Each start runs at most max_iters iterations, or stops when the stress improves by less than tol. Random starts come from a seed argument, and results are identical for any number of cpus. The result’s attributes are stress, converged, n_iters, n_starts, best_start, n_best, and ties.

  • New mds() runs metric multidimensional scaling with the SMACOF algorithm of scikit-learn’s metric MDS(), fitting the distances themselves rather than their ranks. It shares nmds()’s engine, starts, arguments (without ties) and result format, and has no limit on the number of samples. dist_ord(dm, "mds") and "metric MDS" select it; "classical MDS", "pco" and "cmdscale" select pcoa().

  • New isomap() runs an Isomap (isometric feature mapping) ordination: it links each sample to its n_neighbors nearest neighbors (or to those within a radius), replaces each distance with the shortest path through that graph, and runs pcoa() on those geodesic distances, which keeps long ecological gradients straight where pcoa() bends them into an arch. A C port of scikit-learn’s Isomap(metric = "precomputed"), it gives the same geodesic distances and embedding to rounding, breaks ties by sample order, and joins disconnected neighbor graphs at their closest samples, with a warning (vegan::isomap() stops instead; note that its k is the number of neighbors, while isomap()’s n_axes is the number of axes). The neighbor and shortest-path searches run in parallel without an n-by-n matrix, and results are identical for any number of cpus.

  • New tsne() runs t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) on a dist object, as a port of scikit-learn’s TSNE to parallel C. gradient = "auto" uses the exact gradient for up to 500 samples (or more than 3 dimensions) and the Barnes-Hut approximation (a quadtree in 2 dimensions, an octree in 3) above that. It finds nearest neighbors exactly from the distances and never forms an n-by-n matrix. It starts from the PCoA solution by default, sets the learning rate with scikit-learn’s rule (learning_rate = "auto"), stops early once the layout stops improving (at most max_iters iterations; the number run is the n_iters attribute), and lowers perplexity for small datasets. Its layouts match scikit-learn’s and Rtsne::Rtsne()’s in quality. Random starts come from a seed argument, and results are identical for any number of cpus.

  • New umap() runs a uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) on a dist object, following uwot::umap() and its defaults: exact nearest neighbours, smooth-kNN calibration and fuzzy union (identical to uwot’s), a spectral start from the normalized graph Laplacian, and the layout optimization of uwot’s batch mode (batch = TRUE: per-epoch gradients, then Adam), which gives uwot’s coordinates from the same start and seeds. Every stage runs in parallel C, the neighbours straight from the dist triangle without an n-by-n matrix. Random numbers come from a seed argument, and results are identical for any number of cpus. min_dist defaults to the canonical 0.1 (umap-learn’s), not uwot’s 0.01.

  • New permanova() runs a permutational multivariate analysis of variance on a dist object and sample metadata. Like ecodive’s other tests, it takes groups: one value per sample (categories or a numeric covariate), or a column name of data. For several variables, give data and a formula instead: factors, covariates, interactions, and Condition() terms. It gives the same table as vegan::adonis2() (Df, sums of squares, R2, F, and p-values), testing the model as a whole or each term sequentially, marginally, or by contrast, with optional strata. Given the same permutation matrix, its permuted F statistics and p-values are identical to adonis2()’s. It returns a list of class "ecodive_test", like mrpp(): the model’s F, p-value, z-score (as summary(vegan::permustats())) and number of permutations come first, whatever by is, then its R2 and adonis2()’s table, as table. The sums of squares come straight from the dist triangle, without the n-by-n matrices adonis2() builds for each permutation, and permutations run in parallel. On one thread it is 25 to 50 times faster than adonis2() with 200 samples, and 100 to 300 times faster with 1,000. Permutations come from a seed argument, and results are identical for any number of cpus. Like adonis2(), it also takes the distances on the left-hand side of a formula: permanova(dm ~ treatment + ph, data).

  • New mrpp() runs a multi-response permutation procedure on a dist object and each sample’s group, as vegan::mrpp(): the observed and expected weighted mean within-group distance (delta), the chance-corrected within-group agreement A, each group’s mean distance, and a permutation p-value, with group weights 'n', 'n-1' or 'n(n-1)' (vegan’s weight.type 1 to 3) and optional strata. It also gives the standardized effect size z of summary(vegan::permustats()). Given the same permutation matrix, its permuted deltas, p-values and z are those of vegan::mrpp(). Each permutation costs one comparison per pair of samples, read straight from the dist triangle; with 500 samples and 999 permutations it is about 60 times faster than vegan::mrpp() on one thread. Results are identical for any number of cpus. Like ecodive’s other permutation tests, it returns a list of class "ecodive_test" whose statistic, p_value, z and n_perm come first, and as.data.frame() turns it into one row with the same columns for every test.

  • New anosim() runs an analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) on a dist object and each sample’s group, given as a vector or as a column of sample metadata, with optional strata. Given the same permutation matrix, its R statistic, permuted R values and p-value match vegan::anosim()’s. It ranks the distances once, with a radix sort, and then each permutation needs only one pass over the ranks, without the n-by-n matrices vegan::anosim() builds; permutations run in parallel. With 300 samples and 999 permutations it takes under a tenth of a second, against about seven for vegan::anosim(). Results are identical for any number of cpus.

  • New permdisp() tests the homogeneity of multivariate dispersions (PERMDISP), as vegan::betadisper() followed by vegan::permutest(): each sample’s distance to its group’s centroid (the default) or spatial median, each group’s mean distance, and the ANOVA F with a permutation p-value, plus optional pairwise t tests and small-group bias adjustment. Distances to centroids come from the distances within groups alone, with no eigendecomposition: they match betadisper()’s to rounding error, and are about 100 times faster with 1,000 samples. betadisper() defaults to spatial medians instead: pass type = "median" to compare with it. permdisp() solves them exactly, where betadisper()’s optimizer stops at about 1e-5. Given the same permutation matrix, its p-values are identical to permutest()’s. Permutations come from a seed argument, can be restricted to strata, and results are identical for any number of cpus.

  • New mantel() runs a Mantel test of the correlation between two distance matrices (Pearson, Spearman, or Kendall), and new mantel_partial() a partial Mantel test, which removes the effect of a third (given). They give the same statistics as vegan::mantel() and vegan::mantel.partial(), and, given the same permutation matrix, the same permuted statistics and p-values. The second and third matrices may also be numeric vectors, one value per sample (such as age), and samples are matched by name. They add lower-tail and two-sided tests (alternative). Each permutation is one pass over the dist triangle, with no n-by-n matrix (Kendall’s tau-b by Knight’s merge sort rather than cor()’s quadratic count), and permutations run in parallel. Permutations come from a seed argument, and results are identical for any number of cpus.

  • New dist_test(dm, test, groups, data, ...) runs any of these tests by name, as dist_ord() does for ordination methods: dist_test(dm, "mrpp", "treatment", meta) is mrpp(dm, "treatment", meta), and other arguments (such as mantel()’s method) pass through. It checks that the variable is of a kind the test takes: categorical groups for anosim, mrpp and permdisp, numeric values for mantel and mantel_partial (passed as their y), and either for permanova. list_dist_tests() and match_dist_test() list and look up the tests, with forgiving name matching ("adonis2" finds permanova, "betadisper" finds permdisp).

  • permanova(), anosim(), mrpp() and permdisp() take pairwise = TRUE to also compare each pair of groups, as is usual after an overall test across several groups, and p_adjust to adjust the pairs’ p-values for multiple testing: any of stats::p.adjust.methods, Holm’s method by default. permanova(), anosim() and mrpp() rerun the test on each pair’s samples, as q2-diversity’s beta_group_significance(pairwise=True) and pairwiseAdonis’s pairwise.adonis2() do, with the pair’s statistics, z-score, sample size, and raw and adjusted p-values in a pairwise data frame. Given the same permutations, the pairs’ statistics and p-values are identical to vegan’s tests on each pair. Each pair’s random permutations come from seed and the pair, so results are identical for any number of cpus; a supplied permutations matrix is cut down to each pair’s samples. A pair that can’t be tested, such as two groups of one sample, gives NAs with a warning. permdisp()’s pairwise t tests gain p_adjusted and p_adjusted_perm (each of its p-value columns adjusted across the pairs, which vegan::permutest() doesn’t do), and z, n and n_perm columns, so its pairwise table now has more columns than before.

  • One rule aligns every per-sample argument (groups, strata, and the Mantel tests’ y and given) in permanova(), mrpp(), anosim(), permdisp(), mantel(), mantel_partial(), envfit() and dist_test(): with data, a column name or one value per row of data; without it, one value per sample, matched by name when named, else by position. The same checks and messages apply everywhere. As with vegan::adonis2(), permanova() needs groups or a formula (use formula = ~ . to test every column of data). permutations is limited to 1e8.

  • New dbrda() runs a distance-based redundancy analysis (db-RDA): the axes of a dist object that sample metadata explain, given as a formula such as ~ treatment + Condition(site). It gives the same eigenvalues, inertia, site scores, biplot scores and centroids as vegan::dbrda() (up to each axis’s sign; not vegan::capscale(), which differs for non-Euclidean distances), without forming an n-by-n matrix: the constrained axes come from a small eigenproblem, and unconstrained axes (MDS1, …) are only computed when the constraints give fewer than n_axes axes. Its results are identical for any number of cpus. As in vegan, dbrda(dm ~ treatment, data) works too, and a formula of only Condition() terms gives the unconstrained ordination after removing their effect.

  • dbrda() takes the same groups, data and formula as permanova(): one variable as groups (a vector or a column of data), or data and a formula, or dm ~ terms, so dist_ord(dm, "dbrda", "treatment", meta) works. Its results gain r_squared and adj_r_squared, as vegan::RsquareAdj(), including for partial models.

  • New capscale() runs a constrained analysis of principal coordinates. It gives the same results as vegan::capscale() (and phyloseq::ordinate(method = "CAP")), with any imaginary inertia from negative eigenvalues reported in inertia. Euclidean distances take dbrda()’s fast path; otherwise a threaded eigendecomposition makes it about five times faster than vegan::capscale() on one thread. Also available as dist_ord(dm, "capscale", ...).

  • New rda() runs a redundancy analysis of a count table: the axes of the (normalized) table that sample metadata explain (RDA1, …), then principal components of the rest (PC1, …). norm = 'hellinger' or 'chord' gives transformation-based RDA (tb-RDA), and Condition() terms partial RDA. It takes groups, data and formula as dbrda() does (and counts ~ terms, as vegan::rda()), and with no model it is a PCA. It gives the same site scores, species scores (loadings), eigenvalues, inertia, R-squared, biplot scores and centroids as vegan::rda() (up to each axis’s sign), sharing dbrda()’s solver and pca()’s sparse table products, so the table is never made dense: with 3,000 samples and 2,000 taxa it takes half a second where vegan::rda() takes a minute. Results are identical for any number of cpus. Also available as count_ord(counts, "rda", ...). Its permutation test is permanova() of Euclidean distances of the normalized table.

  • New cca() runs a canonical correspondence analysis (ter Braak 1986) of a table of abundances: the correspondence analysis axes, in the chi-square metric, that sample metadata explain (CCA1, …), then correspondence analysis axes of the rest (CA1, …). It takes groups, data and formula as rda() does, including Condition() for partial CCA and counts ~ terms, and with no model it is a correspondence analysis. It gives the same site scores, species scores (loadings), eigenvalues, inertia, R-squared, biplot scores and centroids as vegan::cca() (up to each axis’s sign), and the same permutation-based adjusted R-squared as vegan::RsquareAdj() for the same permutations (permutations and seed), partial CCA included. It shares rda()’s solver, with the chi-square weights, and multiplies the table’s non-zero values only, so a sparse table is never made dense: with 3,000 samples and 2,000 taxa it takes half a second where vegan::cca() takes a minute. Results are identical for any number of cpus. Also available as count_ord(counts, "cca", ...).

  • New ca() runs a correspondence analysis of a table of abundances: the unconstrained ordination in the chi-square metric, with species scores (loadings). It gives the same site scores, species scores, eigenvalues and inertia as vegan::ca() (vegan::cca() without constraints), ade4::dudi.coa() and scikit-bio’s ca() (up to each axis’s sign), and is the same as cca() with no model, whose sparse solver it shares. Results are identical for any number of cpus. Also available as count_ord(counts, "ca"); "CA" selects it, and dist_ord(dm, "ca") points to count_ord().

  • New envfit() fits sample metadata (data) and feature tables (counts, such as taxa abundances) onto any ordination, for biplots: an arrow and r-squared for each numeric variable or feature, the centroid of each factor level, and permutation p-values. It gives the same arrows, r-squared and centroids as vegan::envfit(), and the same p-values for the same permutation matrix. Each permutation costs a few multiply-adds per non-zero value of the table, with no refitting, and sparse tables are never made dense, so thousands of taxa with 999 permutations take well under a second (minutes in vegan). It fits every axis of the ordination by default (vegan fits the first two), and its results are identical for any number of cpus.

  • New procrustes() rotates, reflects, and optionally dilates one ordination to fit another of the same samples, and reports the Procrustes sum of squares, m^2: how similar, say, Bray-Curtis and UniFrac PCoAs (or 16S and metagenomic ones) of the same samples are. It gives the same rotation, translation, dilation, residuals and m^2 as vegan::procrustes() (and the same symmetric m^2 as SciPy’s scipy.spatial.procrustes()), but takes its arguments as procrustes(ord, target): vegan::procrustes(target, ord). vegan’s scale is called dilate. Inputs may be dist objects, ordinated with pcoa() first (n_axes axes), and samples are matched by name. The result is the rotated ordination, with the rest as attributes. New procrustes_test() runs the Procrustes randomization test (PROTEST), giving the same statistic as vegan::protest() and the same p-values for the same permutation matrix, in parallel C, with strata, and identical results for any number of cpus.

  • New plsda() runs a partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA): the components of a count table that best separate known groups, from PLS regression on a dummy matrix of the groups (ported from scikit-learn’s PLSRegression). It gives the same scores, weights, loadings and Y loadings as scikit-learn, and the same scores, explained variance and VIP as mixOmics::plsda() (up to each component’s sign), and also returns each feature’s VIP and each group’s centroid. Each component’s weights are computed directly rather than by NIPALS iteration, so they don’t depend on a convergence tolerance. It takes groups and data as permanova() does, every norm ('clr' is the usual choice for microbiome counts), and sparse tables, which it never makes dense: 1,000 samples and 5,000 taxa take under a tenth of a second, where mixOmics::plsda() takes over a second. Results are identical for any number of cpus. count_ord(counts, 'plsda', groups) runs it too. Like every supervised method, it separates any groups it is given, so validate the separation (e.g. with permanova()).

  • New oplsda() runs an orthogonal PLS discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) of two groups: one predictive component (p1) that separates them and orthogonal components (o1, o2, …) for the rest of the table’s variation (ported from pyopls). It gives the same orthogonal scores, weights and loadings as pyopls, and the same scores, loadings, weights, R2X, R2Y and VIP as ropls::opls() (up to each component’s sign), and also returns each group’s centroid. It takes groups, data, every norm and every table type as plsda() does, and never makes a sparse table dense: 1,000 samples, 5,000 taxa and two orthogonal components take about a tenth of a second, where ropls::opls() takes 8 (including its cross-validation). Results are identical for any number of cpus. count_ord(counts, 'oplsda', groups) runs it too. For more than two groups, use plsda().

  • New lda() runs a linear discriminant analysis (Fisher’s discriminant axes, ported from scikit-learn’s LinearDiscriminantAnalysis with its "svd" solver). It gives the same scores, coefficients (scaling), group means and proportion of trace as MASS::lda() and its predict() (up to each axis’s sign), with optional prior probabilities, and the same scores as scikit-learn up to a constant factor (scikit-learn divides the within-group covariance by n, not n - g). It takes groups and data as plsda() does, every norm and every table type, and stops with an error when the within-group covariance is singular, as it is for microbiome tables with more taxa than samples: run it on a few PCoA or PCA axes instead. 5,000 samples and 200 features take 0.2 seconds, where MASS::lda() takes 0.8. Results are identical for any number of cpus. count_ord(counts, 'lda', groups) runs it too.

  • New simper() runs a similarity percentages analysis (SIMPER): it breaks the mean Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between each pair of groups down into each taxon’s contribution, with its sd, ratio, the groups’ mean abundances and the cumulative proportion, following ecopy’s simper(), and gives each taxon a permutation p-value (Clarke 1993), adjusted within each pair by p_adjust (Holm’s method by default). It gives the same results as vegan::simper() and summary() of it, as one data frame. Its p-values count permuted contributions at least as large as the observed one, as Clarke (1993) does; vegan counts only larger ones, which makes its p-values too small for small groups. As in the pairwise tests, each pair’s permutations shuffle only its own samples (vegan shuffles all of them). It takes groups and data as permanova() does, strata, norm ('none' by default, as vegan) and sparse tables, which it never makes dense, and runs in parallel C: 300 samples and 3,000 taxa, three pairs with 99 permutations, take under 2 seconds on one thread, where vegan::simper() takes 27 seconds for one pair. Results are identical for any number of cpus. Its docs explain why SIMPER’s ranking mixes up differences in mean and in variability (Warton et al. 2012).

  • New bioenv() finds the subset of environmental variables whose distances among the samples best match the community distances (BIOENV; Clarke & Ainsworth 1993): for each subset size, the subset with the highest rank correlation with dm, as one data frame, with the best subset overall as attribute best. It follows scikit-bio’s bioenv() and gives the same subsets and correlations as it and as vegan::bioenv(), with vegan’s options: method (Spearman, Pearson or Kendall), metric ('euclidean', 'mahalanobis', 'manhattan' or 'gower'), max_vars (vegan’s upto) and given (vegan’s partial, also with Kendall, which vegan refuses). Variables come from data, by formula or as its numeric columns, and samples are matched by name. Every subset is searched in parallel C, with no n-by-n matrix: 100 samples and 12 variables (4,095 subsets) take 1.2 seconds on one thread, where vegan::bioenv() takes 5.5. Results are identical for any number of cpus.

  • New varpart() partitions the variation in a community among two to four sets of explanatory variables (Borcard et al. 1992): the fractions each set explains on its own, those they share, and the residuals, from the adjusted R-squared of (partial) RDAs of a count table (with norm, such as "hellinger"), db-RDAs of a dist, or, with chisquare = TRUE, CCAs with permutation-estimated adjusted R-squared (Peres-Neto et al. 2006). It gives the same fractions as vegan::varpart() with two, three and four sets, as one data frame named with vegan’s letters ([a], [b], …), with vegan’s union and conditional fractions as attributes and a text Venn diagram when printed. Each set is a formula over data, a data frame, a matrix, or a vector, matched to the samples by name. For RDA and db-RDA, one pass over the data gives every union’s R-squared, with no n-by-n matrix and sparse tables kept sparse: with 3,000 samples, 2,000 taxa (5% non-zero) and three sets, it takes 0.13 seconds on 4 threads (Hellinger table or Bray-Curtis distances), where vegan::varpart() takes 3.5. Results are identical for any number of cpus.

  • New forward_select() picks explanatory variables one at a time by adjusted R-squared, with a permutation test of each added variable and Blanchet et al.’s (2008) double stopping rule, for RDA of a count table (with norm) or db-RDA of a dist. It selects the same variables in the same order as vegan::ordiR2step(), with the same adjusted R-squared and F, and the same p-values given the same permutations. Candidates are the terms of a formula over data (factors enter whole, interactions after their main effects, Condition() terms are covariables). By default it first tests the global model and selects nothing if that is not significant; max_vars caps the number of variables, and strata restricts permutations. Every candidate’s adjusted R-squared comes from one pass over the data, and only the chosen candidate of each step is tested: with 1,000 samples, 500 taxa, 11 candidates and 199 permutations, it takes 0.17 seconds on 4 threads for the Hellinger table and 0.08 for Bray-Curtis distances, where vegan::ordiR2step() takes 58 and 85. Results are identical for any number of cpus.

  • New alr() and ilr(), the additive and isometric log-ratio transforms, complete the clr and rclr that norm already offers. alr() divides by a denominator feature that you choose (there is no default: scikit-bio uses the first feature and compositions the last). ilr() takes the Helmert basis that scikit-bio uses by default, a sequential binary partition (converted as scikit-bio’s sbp_basis()), or any orthonormal basis, matched to the features by name. Both give the same coordinates as scikit-bio’s alr() and ilr() (alr() to the last bit, ilr() to 1e-15), take every table type with zeros handled by the shared pseudocount rule, and return a dense matrix in the input’s orientation with method, denominator or basis, and pseudocount attributes, ready for pca(), rda(), lda() or envfit(). The default basis is applied by a running sum, without a dense product: 2,000 samples by 5,000 taxa take 0.2 seconds, where normalize(x, 'clr') %*% t(basis) takes 30 with R’s reference BLAS. Euclidean distances on ilr() coordinates are aitchison() distances, for any basis. Results are identical for any number of cpus.

  • New replace_zeros() replaces the zeros of a count table with small positive values, so that log ratios (norm = 'clr', aitchison(), alr(), ilr()) can be taken without a pseudocount: its result has no zeros, so they use none and give no warning. It runs any zero replacement method by name, as count_ord() does for ordinations, and list_zero_replacements() and match_zero_replacement() list and look up the methods. The first is replace_zeros_mult(), multiplicative replacement (Martín-Fernández et al. 2003): every zero becomes delta (one value, or one per sample; scikit-bio’s 1 / D^2 by default) and each sample’s non-zero proportions shrink by the same factor, keeping their ratios. Its results are bit-identical to scikit-bio’s multi_replace(). Every method returns a dense matrix of proportions in the input’s orientation, with method, its parameters and n_replaced attributes, and takes every table type: a sparse 2,000 by 5,000 table takes 0.2 seconds.

  • New log_ratio() and balance() give one log ratio per sample between a numerator and a denominator group of features (names, indices or logical vectors), as a named vector that drops straight into metadata or a test. log_ratio() is the log of the ratio of summed abundances, as Qurro plots it (identical to Qurro’s qarcoal()); it needs no pseudocount by default, and gives NA, with one warning, where a sum is

    1. balance() is the isometric log-ratio balance, the scaled log ratio of geometric means: bit-identical to the matching coordinate of ilr() with a sequential binary partition, and equal to scikit-bio’s to 6e-16, without building the full basis; zeros follow the shared pseudocount rule over the whole table, and the output of replace_zeros() needs none. Both take every table type and keep sparse tables sparse: 2,000 samples by 5,000 taxa take under 0.1 seconds.

  • New vlr(), rho_p() and phi_s() measure proportionality between every pair of features, the compositionally valid alternative to correlating relative abundances (Lovell et al. 2015). vlr() is the variance of the log ratio, equal to scikit-bio’s pairwise_vlr() to 4e-15 but computed from differences rather than a covariance matrix, so nearly proportional pairs keep their precision. rho_p() is Erb & Notredame’s proportionality correlation (propr’s "rho") and phi_s() the symmetric phi of Quinn et al. (propr’s "phs"), against the clr by default or a denominator (one feature, an alr, or a set). Each returns a dist over the features, ready for pcoa() or hclust() (rho_p(), a similarity, for thresholding). They take every table type and keep it sparse, run in parallel, and give identical results for any cpus: all 4.5 million pairs of 3,000 taxa in 500 samples take about a second on 4 cores.

  • New qmp_scale() and qmp_rarefy() turn relative abundances into absolute abundances when each sample’s total microbial load was measured (flow cytometry, qPCR, a spike-in). qmp_scale() multiplies each sample’s relative abundances by its load (Jian et al. 2020); qmp_rarefy() is Vandeputte et al.’s (2017) quantitative microbiome profiling, which first rarefies every sample to the same number of reads per unit of load. It follows the authors’ QMP.R (BSD-3, Raes Lab), with the same sampling depths and targets, but uses ecodive’s own rarefaction and seed. load is matched to the samples by name, or given as a column of data. Both keep the table’s class and orientation, and sparse tables stay sparse: 2,000 samples by 5,000 taxa take under 0.1 seconds.

  • New ancom() runs ANCOM (Mandal et al. 2015), the analysis of composition of microbiomes: it tests every log ratio between two features for a difference between groups (sig_test = 'anova', or 'kruskal'), adjusts each feature’s p-values (p_adjust, Holm by default), and declares the features whose W, the number of their significant log ratios, passes scikit-bio’s cutoff rule. Its W and decisions are identical to scikit-bio’s ancom() in every reference case, including its quirks (each feature’s family includes a 0 for itself; numpy’s cutoffs); the Kruskal-Wallis statistics are bit-identical to SciPy’s and the F statistics more accurate (SciPy’s cancel to 3e-12). It returns a per-feature table (feature, W, reject). Zeros follow the shared pseudocount rule, and the output of replace_zeros() needs none. The tests run in parallel C straight from the (sparse) table, identical for any cpus: all 4.5 million log ratios of 3,000 features in 200 samples take about 3 seconds on 4 cores (10 with 'kruskal').

  • rarefy(depth =) now also takes one depth per sample (matched to the samples by name when named). drop and warn then compare each sample with its own depth. A single depth gives exactly the same results as before.

  • New normalize() returns a count table after any of the transformations that beta_div(), pca() and envfit() apply with their norm argument ('percent', 'chord', 'hellinger', 'binary', 'clr', 'rclr'), with exactly the values they use. It keeps the table’s orientation, dimnames and form: sparse Matrix and slam input stays sparse. norm = 'clr' gives a dense matrix, since every zero gets a value; the functions with a norm argument avoid that copy.

  • New norm = 'hellinger' option, wherever norm is offered (beta diversity metrics, pca(), pcoa_biplot(), envfit() and normalize()): the square root of each sample’s relative abundances. Euclidean distances of the result are Hellinger distances, and pca(counts, norm = 'hellinger') is the usual Hellinger PCA. Negative values are an error.

  • simper() and plsda() now name counts, not dm, when groups, strata or the rows of data don’t match the number of samples.

  • Method names are matched more reliably by match_metric(), match_dist_ord(), match_dist_test() and match_count_ord(), and so by beta_div(), alpha_div(), dist_ord(), dist_test() and count_ord(): a name that is exactly a method’s ID or alias, in any case, now selects it even when it also begins another method’s name. For example, "Jensen" selects jensen rather than stopping as ambiguous with jsd (Jensen-Shannon divergence), and dist_ord(dm, "Mantel") now says to use dist_test().

  • New pca() runs a principal component analysis of a count table, after any of beta_div()‘s normalizations (e.g. norm = 'clr' for an Aitchison PCA), optionally scaling features to unit variance (scale = TRUE). It gives the same scores, loadings, and variances as prcomp() on the normalized table (up to each axis’s sign), but computes only the first few axes, in parallel C, straight from sparse input without making it dense. Its scores equal pcoa()’s on the matching Euclidean or Aitchison distances; its loadings attribute holds the features’ weights. Results are identical for any number of cpus.

  • New rpca() runs a robust Aitchison PCA (Martino et al. 2019) straight from a count table: a robust centered log-ratio transform that treats zeros as missing, OptSpace matrix completion, and a PCA of the completed matrix. It returns sample scores, feature loadings, and the fit’s progress in the shared ordination format (with eig as variances, on pca()’s scale), and optionally gemelli’s distances between samples as a dist object (distances = TRUE). A C port of gemelli’s rpca(), it gives the same results to within rounding error, but works only with the non-zero counts, so sparse tables stay sparse and nothing of size samples by features is formed. It takes every count-table class that pca() takes, and its results are identical for any number of cpus.

  • New blas_threads() gets or sets how many threads R’s BLAS/LAPACK library uses, while R is running. It works with OpenBLAS, Intel MKL, BLIS, and FlexiBLAS, returns NA where the count can’t be read (e.g. R’s reference BLAS or Apple’s Accelerate), and never raises an error, warning, or message. Setting is limited to what is safe: the count is never raised above the library’s own, and OpenMP’s thread count is left as it is. No other ecodive function calls it.

  • Sparse counts with samples in rows (a dgCMatrix with margin = 1), or as triplets (dgTMatrix, slam’s simple_triplet_matrix), are now imported with counting sorts in linear time, instead of a quicksort: 4 s became 0.06 s for a 5000 x 4000 dgCMatrix with 2.5 million non-zero values, and 26 s became 0.3 s for 9.4 million. Every alpha and beta diversity function benefits, and results are unchanged. Out-of-range indices in these inputs are now an error.

  • Sparse counts: explicitly stored zeros are now ignored, and repeated entries of a dgTMatrix summed, as the Matrix package defines them, so every function gives the same results as for the dense matrix (before, norm = 'binary' counted a stored zero as present). Malformed sparse objects (wrong index types or lengths, bad column pointers) are now an error rather than read out of bounds, and tables with more than ~268 million non-zero values no longer overflow an internal size.

  • Threads now come from a pool that lasts the whole session, and jobs are shared out to whichever threads are free. On a machine busy with other processes, multithreaded calls are no longer much slower than single-threaded ones (pcoa() of 2,000 samples: 0.8 s with 6 threads, where restarting threads for every step took 16 s), and small jobs no longer start threads at all. Results are unchanged, and still the same for any cpus.

  • Every function’s cpus is now capped at n_cpus(), the cores available, so that asking for more threads than that costs nothing. Results are the same for any cpus. Without the parallelly package, n_cpus() now returns at most 2 under R CMD check --as-cran, as parallelly’s does.

  • Fixed NA in an integer or logical count table being read as -2147483648: every alpha and beta diversity function now treats it as NA, as it does in a double table. Before, bray() returned -1 for every pair with that sample.

  • Fixed the pairs argument of the beta diversity functions, which counted the columns of counts as samples even when samples are rows (margin = 1, the default). Out-of-range pairs could crash R, and a table with one feature was rejected as having fewer than two samples.

ecodive 2.3.2

  • Fixed aitchison(), and every beta metric called with norm = 'clr', returning NaN (or, for chebyshev(), wrong values) for every sample pair. Two bugs were involved:

    • Data with no zeros (pseudocount 0) hit log(0) * 0, which is NaN.
    • The pseudocount was truncated to an integer in C, so values below 1, including the automatic min(counts[counts > 0]) / 2, became 0, and values like 1.5 were silently rounded down.

  • gower() with norm = 'clr' now computes each feature’s range, and the distance for features absent from both samples, from that feature’s CLR values instead of treating absent features as 0. gower() with negative inputs (e.g. norm = 'rclr') now also uses the full min-to-max range.

ecodive 2.3.1

CRAN release: 2026-11-05

  • read_tree() now handles quoted labels per the Newick standard:

    • '' inside a quoted label is decoded as one literal apostrophe, so 'it''s' is read as it's.
    • Square brackets inside quotes are literal characters rather than comments, so labels like 'o__[Saprospirales]' are no longer truncated.
    • Newlines and whitespace inside quotes are preserved.
    • Comments ([...]) outside of quotes may contain apostrophes.

  • read_tree() raises an informative error, with the position of the problem, for malformed input such as an unclosed quote, comment, or parenthesis. Previously these could return a garbled tree.

  • read_tree()’s parser is now linear-time and non-recursive, making it about 4x faster on a typical 100,000-tip tree and much faster on very deep trees.

ecodive 2.3.0

  • Added ecodive JOSS citation information.
  • New robust_aitchison() beta diversity function.
  • Switch from testthat to dependency-free tinytest for test suite.
  • read_tree fixes for edge cases.

ecodive 2.2.6

CRAN release: 2026-04-14

  • When using CLR normalization:

    • Warns when zeros are detected and pseudocount is NULL.
    • Then continues with pseudocount <- min(counts[counts>0]) / 2.

Breaking Changes

  • norm now defaults to "none" instead of "percent".
  • norm parameter was removed from some beta diversity functions.

ecodive 2.2.4

Breaking Changes

  • The rarefy() function has been simplified:

    • drop = FALSE now returns samples with original counts when sum < depth.
    • drop = TRUE no longer drops zero-sum features - only zero-sum samples.
    • depth can no longer be a fraction (only positive integers now).
    • n_samples parameter has been removed.
    • warn parameter has been added.

ecodive 2.2.3

  • Coerce counts to double before rarefaction.

ecodive 2.2.2

CRAN release: 2026-01-16

  • Drop explicit zeros from sparse matrices after rarefaction.

ecodive 2.2.1

CRAN release: 2025-12-12

  • Corrected CRAN rchk issue.

ecodive 2.2.0

CRAN release: 2025-12-03

  • Dedicated rarefaction backends for dense and sparse matrices.
  • Auto-conversion to col-major sparse matrix for distance/diversity calculations.

ecodive 2.1.0

CRAN release: 2025-09-26

Breaking Changes

  • rescale parameter is superseded by norm parameter.

Fixes

  • alpha_div() and beta_div() will only forward applicable parameters.
  • No longer crashes when pairs = integer(0).
  • pseudocount = NULL correctly selects smallest non-zero count.

ecodive 2.0.0

CRAN release: 2025-09-21

Breaking Changes

  • Input matrix is now samples as rows.
  • Removed weighted parameter.

Added New Diversity Methods

  • Updated Alpha Options: c("ace", "berger", "brillouin", "chao1", "faith", "fisher", "simpson", "inv_simpson", "margalef", "mcintosh", "menhinick", "observed", "shannon", "squares")

  • Updated Beta Options: c("aitchison", "bhattacharyya", "bray", "canberra", "chebyshev", "chord", "clark", "sorensen", "divergence", "euclidean", "generalized_unifrac", "gower", "hamming", "hellinger", "horn", "jaccard", "jensen", "jsd", "lorentzian", "manhattan", "matusita", "minkowski", "morisita", "motyka", "normalized_unifrac", "ochiai", "psym_chisq", "soergel", "squared_chisq", "squared_chord", "squared_euclidean", "topsoe", "unweighted_unifrac", "variance_adjusted_unifrac", "wave_hedges", "weighted_unifrac")
